Exam Type: MRI KNEE RIGHT WO CONTRAST
Exam Date and Time: [DATE] [TIME]
Indication: Right knee pain. [REDACTED].
Comparison: No relevant prior studies available for comparison.

TECHNIQUE:
MRI of the right knee was performed on a 1.5 Tesla system with a dedicated knee coil in three planes (axial, sagittal, and coronal), using a standard non-contrast protocol.

FINDINGS:
OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:
Alignment is anatomic. Focal osteochondral injury at the medial tibial plateau near the medial joint line with adjacent confluent bone marrow edema. No focal osseous lesion. Tricompartmental marginal osteophytosis.

JOINT SPACE:
Small joint effusion. Small leaking Baker's cyst with internal calcific body. Multiple intra-articular bodies, including a 1.1 cm ossific body at the anterior joint recess and a 0.8 cm ossific body at the posterior joint recess. Post arthroscopy scarring of Hoffa's fat pad.

MEDIAL COMPARTMENT:
Medial meniscus: Diffuse complex degenerative tear of the medial meniscus, with maceration and complete radial tear at the posterior horn-posterior root junction. Posterior medial displacement of a meniscal flap in the region of the posterior root. Severe meniscal extrusion.
Medial compartment cartilage: Diffuse articular cartilage irregularity with confluent regions of full-thickness cartilage loss at the weightbearing aspect of the joint.

LATERAL COMPARTMENT:
Lateral meniscus: No tear.
Lateral compartment cartilage: Diffuse articular cartilage irregularity with areas of high-grade fissuring at the weightbearing aspect of the joint.

PATELLOFEMORAL COMPARTMENT:
Patellofemoral compartment cartilage: Confluent full-thickness articular cartilage loss at the lateral patellar facet and lateral trochlea. Articular surface remodeling at the lateral patellar facet. High-grade articular cartilage loss at the medial trochlea and medial facet.

CRUCIATE LIGAMENTS:
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL): No tear.
Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL): No tear.

COLLATERAL LIGAMENTS & POSTEROLATERAL CORNER:
Medial collateral ligament (MCL): Scarring.
Lateral collateral ligament (LCL) complex: Normal.
Posterolateral corner structures: Normal.

EXTENSOR MECHANISM:
Extensor Apparatus: Normal quadriceps tendon. Normal patellar tendon. Fragmentation of the tibial tubercle, reflecting the chronic sequela of remote Osgood-Schlatter disease.
Medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) and patellar retinacula: Normal.
Patellofemoral tracking: Lateral patellar tilt and translation. No patella alta. Tibial tubercle-trochlear groove (TT-TG) distance is 18 mm, borderline elevated.

MUSCLES/TENDONS:
No disproportionate muscle atrophy. Visualized tendons not previously discussed are intact.

SOFT TISSUES:
Nonspecific prepatellar and scattered subcutaneous edema about the knee. No soft tissue mass. Normal popliteal neurovascular bundle.

IMPRESSION:

1.	Small subchondral insufficiency fracture at the medial tibial plateau near the medial joint line with associated confluent bone marrow edema. No significant articular surface depression.
2.	Tricompartmental osteoarthritis, worst at the patellofemoral and medial tibiofemoral compartments, where it is severe. Small knee joint effusion with multiple ossific intra-articular bodies measuring up to 1.1 cm. Small leaking Baker's cyst.
3.	Complex degenerative tearing of the medial meniscus with dominant radial tear at the posterior horn-posterior root junction. Displacement of a meniscal flap to the posteromedial joint recess.

RIGHT KNEE MRI.
Examination protocol: Multiplanar, multisequence.
Findings:
The medial meniscus is extruded 4 mm medially from the knee joint. Volume loss is noted in the meniscus; grade III degeneration is observed in the anterior horn, posterior horn, and body. Grade II degeneration is observed in the anterior horn, posterior horn, and body of the lateral meniscus. Signal change secondary to myxoid degeneration is observed in the anterior cruciate ligament. The posterior cruciate ligament and lateral collateral ligament are normal. Periligamentous edema is observed in the medial collateral ligament. Edema is observed in the prepatellar subcutaneous fat tissue. The distal quadriceps and patellar tendons are normal. The patella is normally positioned. There is no retinacular discontinuity. Mild fluid increase is observed in the suprapatellar bursa. Subcutaneous varicosities are observed in the medial aspect of the crural region near the knee. Joint space narrowing is present in the medial tibiofemoral compartment; a subchondral cyst measuring up to 18x8 mm and bone marrow edema are observed in the medial tibial plateau adjacent to the joint. Loss of cartilage integrity is observed in the femoral and tibial cartilages at this level. Millimetric osteophytic spurring is present at the corners of the bony structures.
CONCLUSION: Gonarthrosis, medial extrusion of the medial meniscus, volume loss and grade III meniscopathy, grade II meniscopathy of the lateral meniscus, myxoid degeneration of the anterior cruciate ligament, grade I sprain of the medial collateral ligament, prepatellar subcutaneous edema, subcutaneous varicosities at the crural level.

JOINT SPACE:
Small joint effusion. No intra-articular bodies. Moderate complex multilobulated Baker's cyst with calcified bodies and synovial proliferation.

MEDIAL COMPARTMENT:
Medial meniscus: Complex degenerative tearing involving the anterior horn, body and posterior horn medial meniscus with severe meniscal extrusion of the body and displaced fragment within the meniscotibial recess. Superimposed reactive marrow edema at the medial tibial margin.
Medial compartment cartilage: Diffuse full-thickness cartilage loss about the weightbearing medial femoral condyle with scattered areas of subchondral marrow edema and cystic change. Additional diffuse cartilage loss along the anterior and central medial tibial plateau with scattered subchondral marrow edema.


LATERAL COMPARTMENT:
Lateral meniscus: Degenerative signal posterior horn and posterior root with suspected degenerative tearing at the posterior horn-posterior root junction. No meniscal extrusion or displaced fragment.
Lateral compartment cartilage: Low-grade partial-thickness cartilage loss/fraying about the central weightbearing lateral femoral condyle.

PATELLOFEMORAL COMPARTMENT:
Patellofemoral compartment cartilage: Focal partial thickness chondrosis central femoral trochlea. Patellar cartilage is intact. 

CRUCIATE LIGAMENTS:
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL): Normal with both bundles intact.
Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL): Normal.

COLLATERAL LIGAMENTS & POSTEROLATERAL CORNER:
Medial collateral ligament (MCL): Bowing of the medial meniscus secondary to adjacent medial meniscal pathology. Otherwise intact.
Lateral collateral ligament (LCL) complex: Grade 1 sprain characterized by periligamentous edema.
Posterolateral corner structures: Normal.

EXTENSOR MECHANISM:
Distal quadriceps tendon: No tendinosis or tear.

No acute muscle strain or muscle atrophy. Visualized tendons not previously discussed are intact without tendinosis or tear.

SOFT TISSUES:
Nonspecific subcutaneous soft tissue edema about the anterior knee. Mild deep infrapatellar bursitis. No soft tissue mass. Normal popliteal neurovascular bundle.

TECHNIQUE: The examination was performed with T1, proton density with fat signal suppression, and T2 gradient echo sequences.

FINDINGS
- An adequate amount of intra-articular fluid collection is identified, particularly in the suprapatellar recess.
- Findings of extensive osteoarthritis are noted with large marginal osteophytes in both compartments, full-thickness articular cartilage erosions with accompanying subchondral changes in the medial compartment and correspondingly partial-thickness in the lateral compartment. There is coexisting loss of meniscal mass in the body of the medial meniscus and diffusely pathological signal in the dislocated posterior horn of the medial meniscus and overall in the lateral meniscus, in the setting of degeneration. Marginal osteophytes are also identified in the patellofemoral articulation, without articular cartilage erosions at the same level.
- Nodular loose bodies up to 7 mm are observed, intra-articularly at the posterior recess, in the setting of secondary osteochondromatosis.
- Confluent-multiloculated parameniscal cysts are identified in the medial aspect, with a total craniocaudal dimension of approximately 3 cm.

MCL.evidence: No mention of the MCL or any medial collateral ligament injury. The medial-sided findings described (parameniscal cysts, meniscal degeneration) do not imply MCL damage.

Examination protocol: Multiplanar, multisequence.
Findings: Grade II degeneration is observed in the anterior horn, posterior horn, and body of the lateral meniscus. The medial meniscus is extruded 5 mm medially in the knee joint. The distal quadriceps and patellar tendons are normal. The patella is normally positioned. There is no retinacular discontinuity. A 2x1 cm extra-articular ganglion cyst is observed in the vicinity of the posterior superior aspect of the medial femoral condyle at the popliteal level. Joint space narrowing in the medial tibiofemoral joint, and thinning of the femoral and tibial cartilages adjacent to the joint are observed. A 1 cm diameter ganglion cyst is observed in the posterior vicinity of the posterior cruciate ligament.
Conclusion: Joint space narrowing in the medial tibiofemoral joint, focal thinning of the cartilages adjacent to the joint, medial extrusion of the medial meniscus, grade III meniscopathy and horizontal tear, grade II meniscopathy of the lateral meniscus, grade I sprain of the medial collateral ligament, extra-articular ganglion cyst in the popliteal fossa, mild suprapatellar bursitis.

Calcifications in the soft tissues dorsal to the tibia are visualized. Conclusion: MR evidence of advanced gonarthrosis, more pronounced on the medial side. Degenerative changes in both menisci. The posterior horn of the medial meniscus is fragmented; the lateral meniscus is extruded laterally. Chronic rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament. Joint effusion with signs of hemarthrosis. MRI Findings:

Left knee joint: MRI findings of pronounced degenerative changes in the left knee joint. The articular cartilage on the medial side is lysed almost entirely. On the lateral side, defects in the articular cartilage are seen in proximity to the intercondylar eminences. The cartilage of the patella is relatively preserved. MRI findings of massive osteophytes on the femoral and tibial condyles. Relatively smaller osteophytes are also visualized at the superior and inferior poles of the patella. The intercondylar eminences are sharpened. Presence of joint effusion. MRI findings of rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament, chronic. The posterior cruciate ligament is intact. Collateral ligaments – unremarkable. Degenerative changes are visualized in both menisci – in the lateral meniscus in the region of the anterior horn, while the medial meniscus is entirely degenerated. The posterior horn of the medial meniscus is fragmented. Presence of mild subchondral bone marrow edema in the femur and tibia on the medial side. Popliteal fossa – a small Baker's cyst is seen with typical location.

Conclusion: MRI findings of gonarthrosis, more pronounced on the medial side. Degenerative change in both menisci. The posterior horn of the medial meniscus is fragmented. Rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament. Joint effusion. Baker's cyst.

Right knee joint: Advanced degenerative changes are also established in the right knee joint, predominantly on the medial side. The congruence of the joint is disrupted, with the joint being subluxated. The articular cartilage on the medial side is entirely lysed. The posterior horn of the medial meniscus is fragmented, with part of the meniscus missing. The anterior horn of the medial meniscus is severely degenerated. The anterior horn of the meniscus is enlarged and with increased signal intensity. A cyst is also seen, associated with the anterior horn of the medial meniscus. The lateral meniscus is relatively preserved. The articular cartilage on the lateral side has irregularities in the contour outlines, corresponding to local defects. MRI findings of osteophytes on the articular ends of the femur and tibia. The intercondylar eminences are sharpened. The cruciate ligaments are intact. Pronounced subchondral bone marrow edema is visualized in the tibia. A loose body (joint mouse) is seen in the joint. The loose body is round in shape and 7 mm in size, located dorsally, adjacent to the joint capsule and medially. Large joint effusion.

Conclusion: MRI findings of advanced gonarthrosis, more pronounced on the medial side of the right knee joint. Degenerative change and rupture of the medial meniscus. Subluxation of the right knee joint. Loose body (joint mouse) in the right knee joint. Joint effusion.

IMPRESSION:

1.	Horizontal tear of the lateral meniscus small perimeniscal cyst. No meniscal extrusion.

text: LEFT KNEE MRI. Examination protocol: Multiplanar, multisequence. Findings: The medial meniscus is extruded 6 mm medially from the knee joint. Grade III degeneration and an accompanying horizontal tear at the free edge are observed in the posterior horn and body of the meniscus. Grade II degeneration is observed in the anterior and posterior horns and body of the lateral meniscus. Loss of integrity secondary to complete rupture is observed in the anterior cruciate ligament. The lateral collateral ligament is normal. Diffuse increase in T2 signal is observed in the posterior cruciate ligament, and grade II sprain is noted. Periligamentous edema is observed in the medial collateral ligament (grade I sprain). A 17x13 mm extra-articular ganglion cyst is observed adjacent to the posterior superior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle. A 6.5 x 1.5 cm Baker's cyst is observed in the popliteal fossa. Subcortical degenerative millimetric cysts are observed at the attachment sites of the cruciate ligaments in the intercondylar notch of the femur and the intercondylar eminence of the tibia. Increased fluid is observed in the suprapatellar bursa and knee joint space. Central-marginal osteophyte formations are observed in all three compartments of the knee joint. Joint space narrowing, thinning and destruction of the femoral and tibial cartilages adjacent to the joint are observed in the medial tibiofemoral compartment. Edema is observed in the subchondral area of the medial tibial plateau. Findings are interpreted in favor of degenerative arthritis. CONCLUSION: Gonarthrosis, medial extrusion and grade III meniscopathy of the medial meniscus, grade II meniscopathy of the lateral meniscus, anterior cruciate ligament rupture, subchondral degenerative cysts in the intercondylar notch of the femur and intercondylar eminence of the tibia, grade I sprain of the medial collateral ligament, Baker's cyst in the popliteal fossa, extra-articular ganglion cyst, sprain of the posterior cruciate ligament.

Interpretation:

In the interval, there has been progression of a moderate to large intra-articular effusion with signs of chronic synovitis. There is also increase in size of a multi-lobulated, uncomplicated Baker's cyst measuring 4.4 cm in CC diameter.

There is a slightly complex tear of the medial meniscus in the interval with a probably oblique longitudinal component at the junction of the posterior horn and meniscal body with a displaced meniscal flap within the anterosuperior recess of the medial femorotibial joint space. There is moderate extrusion of the residual meniscus.

There is progression of a now severe chondropathy (grade 4) in the medial femorotibial compartment with full-thickness cartilage surface denudation and associated reactive subchondral changes. Moderate marginal osteophytes.

The medial collateral ligament is intact without tear.

Mild blunting of the free edge of the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus without significant meniscal tear. Mild to moderate chondral attenuation in the lateral femorotibial compartment with partial chondral fissures consistent with grade 2 chondropathy. There is no evidence of full-thickness involvement or associated reactive subchondral changes. Moderate osteophytosis. The lateral collateral ligament complex is intact without tear. There are multiple ganglion cysts related to the myotendinous junction and popliteal recess on the posterolateral aspect of the knee.

The anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments are intact without tear.

The femoropatellar alignment remains within normal limits. The distal quadriceps and patellar tendons are intact without tear. There is moderate diffuse attenuation of the chondral surfaces, with a similar focus of grade 4 chondropathy along the medial patellar facet with full-thickness fissure and early associated reactive subchondral changes, and grade 3 at the intercondylar notch with full-thickness chondral fissure. Small marginal osteophytes.

Prepatellar and infrapatellar subcutaneous edema, nonspecific.

Conclusion:

There is a new slightly complex interval tear involving the medial meniscus with an oblique longitudinal component at the junction of the posterior horn and meniscal body and a displaced meniscal flap within the anterosuperior recess of the medial femorotibial joint space as described above.

There is progression of femorotibial chondropathy, predominantly medial, with grade 4 involvement.

Progression of an intra-articular effusion now moderate to large and of an uncomplicated Baker's cyst with associated signs of synovitis.

There is no other significant interval change including grade 4 chondropathy along the medial patellar facet.

Exam Type: MRI KNEE RIGHT WO CONTRAST
Exam Date and Time: [DATE] [TIME]
Indication: Approximately 2 weeks of right knee pain after fall while skiing.
Comparison: [REDACTED].

TECHNIQUE:
MRI of the right knee was performed on a 1.5 Tesla system in three planes (axial, sagittal, and coronal), using a standard non-contrast protocol.

FINDINGS:
OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:
There are foci of bone marrow edema at the terminal sulcus of the lateral femoral condyle and posterior lateral tibial plateau consistent with a recent pivot shift type injury. No suspicious bone marrow signal abnormality is identified.

JOINT SPACE:
Alignment is anatomic. There is a small to moderate knee joint effusion. No calcified/ossified intra-articular bodies are identified. Trace Baker's cyst.

MEDIAL COMPARTMENT:
Medial meniscus: Small focus of surfacing signal abnormality (seen best on series 4, image 21 and series 6, image 19), which may represent a small undersurface tear at the junction of the body/posterior horn of the medial meniscus. No extrusion, displaced fragment, or para meniscal cyst is identified.
Medial compartment cartilage: Slight cartilage heterogeneity and fraying along the central weightbearing surface of the medial femoral condyle without discrete high-grade defect. Medial tibial plateau cartilage appears intact.

LATERAL COMPARTMENT:
Lateral meniscus: Intact.
Lateral compartment cartilage: Focal, mild cartilage fraying along the posterior/central lateral tibial plateau.

PATELLOFEMORAL COMPARTMENT:
Patellofemoral compartment cartilage: No focal cartilage defects.

CRUCIATE LIGAMENTS:
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL): Markedly edematous and enlarged with near complete/complete mid substance disruption.
Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL): Intact.

MRI OF THE RIGHT KNEE

TECHNIQUE
The examination was performed with T1, T2 gradient echo, and proton density pulse sequences with fat signal suppression.

FINDINGS
Evaluation of the lateral compartment reveals small marginal osteophytes as well as mild degeneration of the meniscus without tear.

In the medial compartment, significant degenerative osteoarthritis is observed with complete erosion of the articular cartilage (ICRS grade 4), degenerative tear of the meniscus and extrusion of the remaining meniscal material, presence of marginal osteophytes and subarticular bone marrow lesions on both sides.

Evaluation of the anterior compartment reveals complete erosion of the articular cartilage at the inferomedial aspect of the articular surface of the patella.

Intra-articularly, multiple loose bodies are observed posterior to the posterior cruciate ligament, as well as the presence of foci of lipoma arborescens extending into the suprapatellar recess.

Evaluation of the bone marrow reveals a benign enchondroma in the proximal tibial epiphysis.

Incidentally, enthesophytes are noted at the intercondylar notch, the largest of which is in contact with the anterior cruciate ligament, which demonstrates mucoid degeneration. Small ganglion cysts are observed in the anterior articular compartment and larger ganglion cysts posterior to the distal femoral metaphysis.

MRI LEFT KNEE:

INDICATION:    Clicking, locking, exclude meniscal tear..

PRIOR IMAGING: None.
.
TECHNICAL INFORMATION AND PROTOCOL:

Proton density and T2 weighted sagittal, coronal and axial imaging was performed through the knee including a 3D Fat suppressed proton density weighted sequence. No contrast was administered.

FINDINGS:

The 3-D proton density sequence was reformatted and manipulated to aid in the interpretation of this examination. The extensor mechanism is intact. There is patella alta. The Insall Salvati ratio measures about 1.6.
The finding is associated with advanced patellofemoral joint osteoarthritic change with extensive denuding of the articular cartilage and with extensive subcortical cyst formation particularly seen along the apex and lateral facet of patella. Prominent trochlear and patellar osteophytes are demonstrated.

The medial patellar retinaculum is attenuated likely related to previous lateral dislocation and partial disruption. The lateral patellar retinaculum is intact.

There is a degenerative medial meniscal tear. There is maceration and linear signal seen in the posterior horn extending into the body. An oblique inferiorly surfacing tear of the body and posterior horn is a demonstrated. The finding is associated with severe chondral denuding and exuberant marginal osteophyte formation seen to the medial joint compartment. There is also subcortical edema seen to the weightbearing surface of the medial femoral condyle and medial tibial plateau.

The lateral meniscus is macerated and not identified at the body and posterior horn. Findings are in keeping with extensive maceration and degenerative tearing of the body and the posterior horn of lateral meniscus. The finding is associated with denuding of the entire articular cartilage of lateral joint compartment associated with prominent lateral joint compartment osteophyte formation. There is also subcortical sclerosis and mild edema seen within the lateral joint compartment. An intraosseous cyst is seen to the lateral femoral condyle with 3 cm in keeping with subcortical tear.

The anterior cruciate ligament and posterior cruciate and medial collateral ligament are intact.

The lateral collateral ligament complex including the IT band, fibular collateral ligament, biceps femoris tendon and popliteus tendon appear intact.

There is a large knee effusion with reactive synovitis. There is no significant Baker's cyst. In the lateral popliteal fossa there is a large intraosseous loose body projecting anterior to the proximal fibers of the lateral head of the gastrocnemius measuring about 2.4 cm in maximum dimension. Smaller loose bodies are likely present in this region.

INTERPRETATION: 

Severe tricompartmental osteoarthritic change most severely affecting patellofemoral and lateral compartments. Degenerative meniscal tears laterally and medially with cartilaginous denuding to the lateral medial and patellofemoral compartments.

Loose bodies.

Patella alta with attenuation of the medial patellar retinaculum likely related to prior transient lateral dislocation of the patella.

MRI OF THE RIGHT KNEE

TECHNIQUE
The examination was performed with T1, proton density with fat signal suppression, and T2 gradient echo pulse sequences.

FINDINGS
On evaluation of the lateral meniscus, the cruciate and collateral ligaments, and the articular cartilage, no significant findings are observed.
The medial meniscus shows abnormal signal, discontinuity at the posterior horn, and subluxation with abnormal signal in the body.
Bone marrow edema in the medial tibial condyle is attributed to the meniscal tear.
Additionally, intra-articularly, thickening of the synovial membrane is identified, which is also observed within the Baker's synovial cyst at the medial popliteal fossa, while simultaneously a subcortical cystic lesion is demonstrated adjacent to the insertion of the posterior cruciate ligament and an edematous lesion subcortically at the tibial eminence.

CONCLUSION:
1. Degenerative tear of the medial meniscus.
2. Synovitis within a moderate joint effusion in the knee joint, with the presence of focal edema and cystic lesions, raises suspicion of inflammatory arthritis and therefore rheumatological evaluation is recommended.

Complete anterior cruciate ligament tear with anterior tibial drawer.

Findings:

There is a small intra-articular effusion with a small unruptured popliteal cyst.

There are severe degenerative changes at the patellofemoral compartment with complete cartilage loss at the lateral facet and the lateral portion of the femoral trochlea with subchondral reactive changes most prominent at the patella. There are also mild to moderate degenerative changes of the medial compartment with cartilage thinning and loss most prominent at the central portion of the medial femoral condyle. There is also mild thinning and superficial fibrillation of the cartilage of the lateral compartment.

There are intrasubstance degenerative changes involving the body and posterior horn of the medial meniscus. There is a superimposed horizontal tear. The tear extends from the posterior horn to the body. The tear extends to the inferior articular surface of the meniscus. There is no displaced fragment. There is a small parameniscal cyst adjacent to the posterior horn. The lateral meniscus demonstrates intrasubstance degenerative changes involving the body without a well-defined linear tear.

Otherwise, the anterior cruciate ligament, the posterior cruciate ligament, the extensor mechanism, the medial collateral ligament, the semimembranosus, the popliteus muscle and tendon, the distal biceps femoris, the lateral collateral ligament and the iliotibial band are unremarkable.

Conclusion:

1. Degenerative changes involving all three compartments, most prominent at the patellofemoral compartment as detailed above.

2. Intrasubstance degenerative changes of the menisci with superimposed horizontal tear of the medial meniscus as detailed above.

3. Small intra-articular effusion with small popliteal cyst.

TECHNIQUE
The examination was performed with T1, proton density with fat signal suppression, and T2 gradient echo pulse sequences.

FINDINGS
On evaluation of the lateral meniscus, articular cartilage, lateral collateral ligament, posterior cruciate ligament, and bone marrow, no pathological findings are observed.

The medial collateral ligament shows thickening at the femoral attachment, without edema.

A small fluid collection is observed intra-articularly.

2. Vertical tear of the medial meniscus at the body and posterior horn.
3. Old healed partial injury of the medial collateral ligament.
4. The edema in Hoffa's fat pad is attributed to mild impingement syndrome of the patellar tendon against the anterior distal femur.

text: [DATE]: * MRI Right Knee 15ch AA : Clinical Information: Right knee pain. Diagnostic question: Evaluation. Scan protocol (DRB): sagittal intermediate-weighted sequences without and with fat suppression, axial/coronal PD-weighted sequences with fat suppression, coronal T1-weighted sequences. Findings: - No significant distension of the suprapatellar bursa, limited to mildly increased amount of fluid in the semimembranosus/gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa. - Chondromalacia of the medial femorotibial compartment with global cartilage loss as well as grade 4 cartilage defects, subchondral insufficiency fracture both tibial and femoral (with significant perilesional edema and periosteal soft tissue infiltration extending to the metaphysis). - Complex (partial to sub)total tear/maceration of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus (near the posterior meniscal root) with extra-articular extrusion of the body portion, also characterized by an undersurface tear and locoregional mucoid degeneration. - Grade 1 sprain pattern of the MCL, secondary to the above-described findings. Furthermore: "Full thickness" cartilage loss/denudation of the medial patellar facet and patellar ridge (extending to the lateral facet, partially undermined) - associated sharpening of the joint margins. Conclusion: Gonarthrosis (as described above) with a degenerative tear of the medial meniscus - secondary to this, subchondral insufficiency fractures of the medial femorotibial compartment.

ACL.evidence: The ACL is not mentioned anywhere in the report. The described pathology is entirely degenerative (medial compartment OA, degenerative meniscal tear, insufficiency fractures), making an ACL tear unlikely but not explicitly excluded.

MCL.evidence: Grade 1 sprain pattern of the MCL, secondary to the above-described findings.

Medial Meniscus.evidence: Complex (partial to sub)total tear/maceration of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus (near the posterior meniscal root) with extra-articular extrusion of the body portion, also characterized by an undersurface tear and locoregional mucoid degeneration.

Lateral Meniscus.evidence: The lateral meniscus is not mentioned. All described meniscal pathology is confined to the medial meniscus. No indirect evidence of a lateral meniscal tear.

Medial OA.evidence: Chondromalacia of the medial femorotibial compartment with global cartilage loss as well as grade 4 cartilage defects, subchondral insufficiency fracture both tibial and femoral (with significant perilesional edema and periosteal soft tissue infiltration extending to the metaphysis).

Synovitis.evidence: Not explicitly stated, but the report describes 'periosteal soft tissue infiltration extending to the metaphysis' and a severely degenerative joint with grade 4 defects and insufficiency fractures, which commonly incites reactive synovitis. No direct mention of synovial thickening or enhancement.

Contusion.evidence: The 'significant perilesional edema' is described in the context of subchondral insufficiency fractures secondary to degenerative cartilage loss, not a traumatic bone bruise. Per scoring rules, subchondral marrow oedema adjacent to a degenerative cartilage defect is not a contusion.

The examination was performed with T1, T2 gradient echo and proton density pulse sequences with fat signal suppression.

A small fluid collection is observed in the knee joint. text:
Findings:

Moderate intra-articular effusion, with suspicion of a fat-fluid level on the lateral side suggesting a degree of lipohemarthrosis. No significant Baker's cyst, with a thin rim of fluid within the popliteal fossa and the proximal portion of the pes anserinus.

There is blunting of the posterior margin of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus, suspicious for a potential peripheral vertical longitudinal tear. There is also relatively significant extrusion of the meniscal body, most likely related to a complete tear of the medial collateral ligament.

There is a complete tear of the distal medial collateral ligament with proximal retraction of the torn fibers, associated with multiple zones of irregularity, thickening, and abnormal intrasubstance signal. There is also attenuation and intrasubstance signal at its origin. The torn distal portion of the medial collateral ligament is situated slightly beneath the pes anserinus tendons, constituting a "pseudo-Stener" type lesion. There is also a complete tear of the deep meniscofemoral component and a partial tear of the meniscotibial component.

No full-thickness chondral defect of the medial femorotibial compartment.

The lateral meniscus is intact without tear. There is a small fracture on the superior aspect of the fibular head, potentially at the insertion of the arcuate popliteal ligament. Minimal displacement and associated edema. The distal insertion of the lateral collateral ligament and the biceps tendon is preserved, as is the origin. There is also a small ossification on the posterior aspect of the fibular head measuring 5 mm, of indeterminate origin.

There are subchondral bone irregularities at the weight-bearing surface of the lateral femoral condyle, appearing rather chronic. No full-thickness chondral defect of the lateral femorotibial compartment. However, a small focus of edema on the posterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle with mild chondral hyperintensity, contusion versus osteochondral lesion (atypical) versus stress change related to the origin of the lateral gastrocnemius.

Ganglion cyst at the origin of both gastrocnemii.

There is a tear appearing complete at the distal insertion of the posterior cruciate ligament and/or PCL avulsion. The ligament is proximally retracted, thickened, and of abnormal signal. There is significant attenuation of the anterior cruciate ligament without a full-thickness component noted, however, consistent with a partial tear. There are contusions likely involving the lateral tibial plateau, more marked posteriorly +/- impaction/subchondral fracture.

Small ganglion cyst at the distal footprint of the anterior cruciate ligament.

Patellofemoral alignment remains within normal limits. Sequelae of Osgood-Schlatter disease with chronic-appearing fragmentation of the tibial tuberosity and mild thickening of the patellar tendon. The distal quadriceps tendon is intact without tear. No full-thickness chondral defect of the patellofemoral compartment. Hoffa's fat pad is unremarkable.

There is significant diffuse subcutaneous and intermuscular edema. There is also edema of the popliteus and plantaris muscles consistent with a sprain.

Conclusion:

Complete tear of the distal medial collateral ligament with displacement of the distal portion beneath the pes anserinus tendons, consistent with a "pseudo-Stener" type lesion. There is also a complete tear of the deep meniscofemoral component and a partial tear of the meniscotibial component.

Tear appearing complete of the distal posterior cruciate ligament and/or PCL avulsion. Probable partial tear of the anterior cruciate ligament.

Fracture of the superior aspect of the fibular head, probably at the insertion of the arcuate popliteal ligament. Associated edema.

Additionally, probable contusions of the lateral tibial plateau +/- impaction/subchondral fracture and of the posterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle.

Blunting of the posterior margin of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus, suspicious for a potential peripheral vertical longitudinal tear.

Moderate intra-articular effusion with suspected lipohemarthrosis component.

In this context, further investigation with CT is recommended to better evaluate the bony structures. Additionally, an orthopedic surgery consultation is also strongly recommended.

The posterior cruciate ligament, lateral collateral ligament, and medial collateral ligament are normal. Signal change secondary to myxoid degeneration is observed in the anterior cruciate ligament. A subchondral millimetric cyst and signal change consistent with edema in its vicinity are observed at the anterior aspect of the tibial intercondylar eminence. A subchondral osteochondral defect measuring 6.5 x 4.5 mm is observed at the anterior aspect of the femoral intercondylar area. The distal quadriceps and patellar tendons are normal. The patella is normally positioned. There is no retinacular discontinuity. Minimal fluid increase is observed in the suprapatellar bursa and knee joint space. Osteophytic spurring is observed at the corners of the bony structures at the tibiofemoral joint level. Joint space narrowing is observed in the medial tibiofemoral joint. Focal thinning is observed in the femoral and tibial cartilages adjacent to the joint.

Interpretation:

There is a minimal rim of fluid within the suprapatellar recess, without significant intra-articular effusion. There is a small Baker's cyst, without significant complication, measuring 2.8 cm in CC diameter.

There is a horizontal longitudinal tear involving the posterior horn and body of the medial meniscus, extending to the posterior root, to the junction with the anterior horn and along the inferior articular surface. There are small parameniscal cysts associated on the posterior aspect.

There is thickening of the superficial fibers of the medial collateral ligament with mild to moderate surrounding edema suggesting a grade 1 sprain.

There is mild to moderate attenuation of the chondral surfaces in the medial femorotibial compartment, without full-thickness involvement. There are small marginal osteophytes.

The lateral meniscus and the lateral collateral ligament complex are intact and without tear.

There is mild to moderate diffuse attenuation of the chondral surfaces in the lateral femorotibial compartment with a focus of severe chondropathy at the non-weight-bearing surface on the posterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle with focal full-thickness loss of the cartilage surface and early associated reactive subchondral changes. There are minimal marginal osteophytes.

The anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments are intact and without tear. There are minimal intraosseous ganglion cysts beneath the distal insertion of the anterior cruciate ligament.

The patellofemoral alignment appears within normal limits. There are several magnetic susceptibility artifacts on the anterior aspect of the patellar tendon, most likely of post-interventional/surgical nature; to correlate clinically.

The distal quadriceps and patellar tendons are grossly intact and without tear.

There is mild prepatellar thickening which could be related to sequelae of bursitis.

There is mild attenuation of the chondral surfaces in the patellofemoral compartment, mainly at the trochlear surface with foci of severe chondropathy along the intercondylar notch and the lateral trochlear facet with full-thickness fissures and associated reactive subchondral changes. There are small marginal osteophytes.

There are millimetric ganglion microcysts related to the proximal tibiofibular joint.

Conclusion:

Horizontal longitudinal tear of the posterior horn and body of the medial meniscus as described above with small parameniscal cysts associated on the posterior aspect.

Grade 1 sprain of the medial collateral ligament.

Tricompartmental degenerative changes/chondropathy with foci of severe chondropathy at the non-weight-bearing surface on the posterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and along the trochlear surface in the patellofemoral compartment.

No significant intra-articular effusion.

Small uncomplicated Baker's cyst.

Other findings as described above.

None.

Spin echo sequence were used.

There are increased intrasubsance signal intensity in posterior horn of medial meniscus and anterior horn of lateral meniscus on proton density sequence, R/O tear.

Subcutaneous infiltration is noted at infrapatellar area to pretibial area.
Presence of fissure of medial aspect lateral facet of patella extending to subchondral bone in favor of grade 2 chondromalacia.
The contour of PCL appear to be within normal, no abnormal signal intensity is noted.
Both medial and lateral collateral ligaments appear to be within normal.
No evidence of bone contusion is noted.

Impression:
1. Compatible with a Baker's cyst associated with adjacent soft tissue infiltrations.
2. Massive effusion with synovitis and with/without lipoma arborescence.
3. In favor of grade 2 chondromalacia of medial aspect lateral facet of patella.
4. Suspected tear of posterior horn of medial meniscus and anterior horn of lateral meniscus.
Suggest correlation with clinical manifestation.

The cruciate ligaments are intact. There is a moderate thickening with associated T2 hyperintensity of the proximal medial collateral ligament. Otherwise the collateral ligaments are intact. The extensor mechanism of the knee is unremarkable.

There are no deep cartilage defects in the medial and lateral femorotibial joint compartment. 

There is an mild chondrosis at the medial and lateral patellar facet with focal superficial cartilage irregularities at the lateral patellar facet. There are no cartilage defects, no subchondral bone marrow edema.

There is no joint effusion. There is no Baker's cyst. 

The joint articulations are well-maintained. 

There is a lobulated ganglion cyst extending along the popliteus tendon measuring 4.5 x 1.4 cm in the axial plane.

The infrapatellar fat pad is unremarkable. The visualized muscle bulk is intact.

Conclusion:
1. Radial tear of the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus. No displaced meniscal fragments. 
2. No acute ligamentous injury, especially no tear of the lateral collateral ligament.
3. Mild patellofemoral chondrosis.

text:
FINDINGS:

There is a large knee joint effusion. There is significant soft tissue swelling surrounding the knee.

There is complete tear of the anterior cruciate ligament. There is thickening and increased signal involving the distal posterior cruciate ligament with partial tear (approximately 50% of the fibers) of the posterior medial fibers. There is mild thickening and increased signal involving the proximal and mid aspect of the PCL.

There is complete radial tear of the posterior root of the lateral meniscus. The medial meniscus is unremarkable.

There is complete tear of the medial collateral ligament with distal avulsion of the superficial component which is retracted proximally and superficial to the pes anserine tendons compatible with a pseudoStener lesion. There is also high-grade injury involving the deep meniscal femoral and meniscal tibial component of the MCL with thickening of the posterior oblique ligament.

There is almost complete tear of the lateral collateral ligament at its femoral attachment. There are thinned out fibers that appear physically continuous. This is likely a functionally complete tear. There is also almost complete tear of the popliteus tendon as it courses around the lateral femoral condyle with significant thinning and laxity of the tendon. There is disruption of the popliteal fibular ligament. The distal biceps femoris insertion remains intact.

There is significant bone marrow edema at the posterior tibial plateau fractures. There is also bone contusion involving the anterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and minimal contusion at the medial femoral condyle.

There is an enchondroma in the distal femur.

CONCLUSION:

1. Complete tear of the ACL with a moderate grade injury of the PCL.

2. High-grade injury involving the medial collateral ligament including distal avulsion of the superficial MCL with pseudo Stener lesion.

3. High-grade tear of the lateral collateral ligament which is likely functionally complete.

4. Almost complete tear of the popliteus tendon. Injury to the popliteal fibular ligament.

5. Complete radial tear involving the posterior root of the lateral meniscus.

6. Significant bone marrow edema surrounding the known tibial plateau fracture with a bone contusion in the lateral femoral condyle.

7. large knee joint effusion.

MRI  KNEE  -  LEFT

TECHNIQUE:  Unenhanced multiplanar multisequence MR images of the knee.

CLINICAL INDICATION:  Fall onto left knee while downhill skiing 3 months ago. Immediate bruising. Has had residual swelling and medial joint line pain. X-ray is negative for OA. Please evaluate for meniscal or ligamentous pathology.

COMPARISON:  None.

FINDINGS:

Nondiagnostic scout images were reviewed.

Radial tear posterior horn and adjacent posterior root of the medial meniscus with slight peripheral extrusion of the medial meniscal body. The anterior horn is intact. The lateral meniscus is intact.

ACL, PCL MCL and LCL are intact.

MCL and LCL are intact. Mild popliteus tendinosis without tear.

Low-grade partial thickness tear of the medial patellofemoral ligament. No patellofemoral subluxation. The lateral patellar retinaculum is intact. No femoral trochlear dysplasia. The TT-TG distance measures 8 mm, within normal limits.

Nonspecific subchondral insufficiency fracture peripheral weightbearing aspect medial femoral condyle, measuring 8 mm anterior to posterior and 6 mm medial to lateral. Exuberant surrounding marrow edema. No evidence of displaced 1 stable osteochondral fragment.

Focal fissuring of articular cartilage central weightbearing aspect medial femoral condyle as well as central to medial femoral trochlea and along the patellar apex and medial patellar facet.

Incidental finding 0.8 x 1.1 x 1.3 cm lowT1 signal intensity and high T2 signal intensity lesion, likely to represent an enchondroma.

3.5 x 1.3 x 2.7 cm the Baker's cyst. Trace fluid in the pes anserine bursa.

Small volume joint effusion.

INTERPRETATION:

1. Radial tear posterior root and posterior horn of the medial meniscus slight extrusion. 
2. Nonspecific subchondral insufficiency fracture medial femoral condyle with exuberant surrounding marrow edema.
3. Medial femorotibial and patellofemoral chondrosis most pronounced involving the patellofemoral compartment suggesting evolving mild patellofemoral predominant osteoarthritis of the left knee. 
4. Low-grade partial thickness tear of the medial patellofemoral ligament without patellofemoral subluxation. 
5. Mild pes anserine bursitis.
6. Incidental finding of enchondroma.

TECHNIQUE
The examination was performed with T1, proton density with fat suppression, and T2 gradient echo pulse sequences.

FINDINGS
From the evaluation of the menisci, the cruciate and collateral ligaments, and the bone marrow, no significant findings are observed.

From the evaluation of the articular cartilage, a small focus of swelling is noted on the medial articular surface of the patellar cartilage, corresponding to chondromalacia. No erosions are observed.

From the evaluation of the remaining extensor mechanism, a focus of edema is recognized in the region of the superior Hoffa's fat pad, where a small synovial plica is also noted infrapatellarly. The finding is consistent with impingement of the inferior pole of the patella against the femur.

A small fluid collection is observed intra-articularly.

In the lateral compartment, edema is observed adjacent to the lateral femoral epicondyle, approximately 3 cm in craniocaudal diameter. The finding is attributed to iliotibial band friction syndrome.

TECHNIQUE: The examination was performed with T1, proton density with fat signal suppression, and T2 gradient echo sequences.

FINDINGS
- Extensive bone marrow edema is observed in the medial femoral condyle and on the medial tibial plateau, with a subarticular low-signal lesion on all sequences. A similar, smaller lesion is observed in the medial tibial condyle. There is only subtle flattening of the articular surface of the medial femoral condyle. The remaining articular surfaces are intact.
- Abnormal signal is observed in the posterior horn and body of the medial meniscus with contour abnormality and subluxation.
- Osteoarthritis is observed with erosion of the articular cartilage of the medial femoral condyle and medial tibial plateau, as well as with the presence of osteophytes. Early osteoarthritis is observed in the lateral patellofemoral compartment.
- Thickening and abnormal signal of the medial collateral ligament at its midportion and toward its femoral insertion, likely reactive to the displacement of the medial meniscus.
- Moderate amount of intra-articular fluid with mild synovitis.

CONCLUSION
1. Findings consistent with insufficiency fracture of the medial femoral and tibial condyles (synonym: "spontaneous osteonecrosis").
2. Degenerative tear of the medial meniscus with joint effusion.

Fracture.evidence: Findings consistent with insufficiency fracture of the medial femoral and tibial condyles (synonym: 'spontaneous osteonecrosis').

MRI RIGHT KNEE:

INDICATION:    [Age] female with right knee pain to the lateral joint line and infrapatellar pain after injury. Rule out meniscal tear.

PRIOR IMAGING: None.
.
TECHNICAL INFORMATION AND PROTOCOL:

Proton density and T2 weighted sagittal, coronal and axial imaging was performed through the knee including a 3D Fat suppressed proton density weighted sequence. No contrast was administered.

FINDINGS:

The 3-D proton density sequence was reformatted and manipulated to aid in the interpretation of this examination.

The extensor mechanism is intact. There is prepatellar edema which may correlate clinically with prepatellar bursitis.

 The Insall Salvati ratio measures about 1.4 consistent with mild patella alta. There is some attenuation of the medial patellar retinaculum with slight lateral subluxation of the patella. Findings may relate to remote injury related to transient lateral dislocation of the patella.

There is chondral fissuring and chondral loss seen to the patellar apex and lateral facet associated with subcortical cyst formation in the patella and with edema. The articular cartilage of the femoral trochlea demonstrates mild chondral fissuring seen at the trochlear apex but is otherwise reasonably well-maintained. The TT TG distance measures about 9 mm, within normal limits.

The lateral meniscus is intact. The articular cartilage of the lateral joint compartment is well-maintained.

The medial meniscus contains some mild non-surfacing signal in the posterior horn and body but demonstrates no surfacing meniscal tear.

The articular cartilage of the medial joint compartment is reasonably well-maintained.

The anterior cruciate ligament, posterior cruciate ligament, medial collateral ligament and lateral collateral ligament complex including IT band, fibular collateral ligament, popliteus tendon and biceps femoris tendon all appear intact and unremarkable.

There is a multiloculated ganglion cyst seen within the popliteal fossa posterior to the posterior cruciate ligament. This measures 2.9 cm in height, and 1.1 by 0.8 cm in short axis. It is situated anterior to the lateral fibers of the medial head of the gastrocnemius.

There is no significant Baker's cyst. There is no evidence of significant knee effusion.

Marrow signal is otherwise within normal limits.

INTERPRETATION: 

Patella alta.

Severe chondromalacia patella. Associated attenuation of the medial patellar retinaculum, possibly related to remote transient lateral patellar dislocation.

Prepatellar bursitis.

Popliteal fossa ganglion cyst as described.

No evidence of internal derangement.

Findings:

There is a small intra-articular effusion without a significant popliteal cyst.

There are mild to moderate degenerative changes involving all three compartments, more prominent in the medial compartment where there is moderate cartilage thinning at the medial femoral condyle and tibial plateau. There is mild cartilage thinning involving the lateral compartment.

At the patellofemoral compartment, there is moderate thinning at the central and medial portion of the femoral trochlea.

There are intrasubstance degenerative changes involving the medial meniscus. There is a complex multidirectional tear involving the body and posterior horn. There is a horizontal component extending from the posterior horn to the level of the body. There is a displaced meniscal fragment from the posterior horn displaced anterior to the posterior root. There is also a displaced fragment at the level of the meniscal body with extrusion. The lateral meniscus demonstrates intrasubstance degenerative changes without a well-defined linear tear.

Otherwise, the anterior cruciate ligament, the posterior cruciate ligament, the extensor mechanism, the medial collateral ligament, the semimembranosus, the popliteus muscle and tendon, the distal biceps femoris, the lateral collateral ligament, and the iliotibial band are unremarkable.

Conclusion:

1. Mild degenerative changes, more prominent at the medial compartment.

2. Progression of the medial meniscal tear with a complex multidirectional tear with multiple displaced fragments (flap-type component) as detailed above.

3. Small intra-articular effusion without a popliteal cyst.

ACL.evidence: Otherwise, the anterior cruciate ligament, the posterior cruciate ligament, the extensor mechanism, the medial collateral ligament, the semimembranosus, the popliteus muscle and tendon, the distal biceps femoris, the lateral collateral ligament, and the iliotibial band are unremarkable.

Medial Meniscus.evidence: There is a complex multidirectional tear involving the body and posterior horn. There is a horizontal component extending from the posterior horn to the level of the body. There is a displaced meniscal fragment from the posterior horn displaced anterior to the posterior root.

Lateral Meniscus.evidence: The lateral meniscus demonstrates intrasubstance degenerative changes without a well-defined linear tear.

Medial OA.evidence: There are mild to moderate degenerative changes involving all three compartments, more prominent in the medial compartment where there is moderate cartilage thinning at the medial femoral condyle and tibial plateau.

Lateral OA.evidence: There is mild cartilage thinning involving the lateral compartment.

PF OA.evidence: At the patellofemoral compartment, there is moderate thinning at the central and medial portion of the femoral trochlea.

Effusion.evidence: There is a small intra-articular effusion without a significant popliteal cyst.

Synovitis.evidence: No explicit mention of synovitis; however, a complex displaced meniscal tear with effusion and tricompartmental degenerative changes make mild reactive synovitis plausible.

Baker's.evidence: There is a small intra-articular effusion without a significant popliteal cyst.

Contusion.evidence: No bone marrow oedema or contusion is described; the degenerative changes are chronic in nature.

3. Joint effusion with mild synovitis is observed.

2. In the lateral and anterior (patellofemoral) compartments, findings of mild degenerative osteoarthritis are observed.
3. On evaluation of the bone marrow, apart from benign hyperplasia at the distal diaphysis of the femur, there is also presence of cystic elements, subarticularly at the mid-portion of the tibial metaphysis with perilesional bone marrow edema. The finding corresponds to degenerative cysts.
4. Intra-articularly, a large fluid collection with mild synovitis and presence of loose bodies is observed, the largest of which has a diameter of 1.5 cm, in the setting of secondary synovial osteochondromatosis.

Findings: A bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus was observed. There is also accompanying grade III degeneration in the posterior horn and body segments. Grade II degeneration was observed in the anterior horn and body segments of the lateral meniscus. Loss of continuity secondary to complete rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament was observed. The posterior cruciate ligament, lateral and medial collateral ligaments are normal. The distal quadriceps and patellar tendons are normal. The patella is normally positioned. There is no retinacular discontinuity. Increased fluid was observed in the suprapatellar bursa and knee joint space. A Baker's cyst measuring 5.5x2 cm was observed in the popliteal fossa.
Conclusion: Complete rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament. Bucket-handle tear and grade III meniscopathy of the medial meniscus. Grade II meniscopathy of the lateral meniscus. Suprapatellar bursitis, mild synovitis of the knee joint. Baker's cyst in the popliteal fossa.

TECHNIQUE
Sections were obtained in T1 and T2/PD sequences in three planes.

FINDINGS
- Diffusely abnormal signal within the fibers of the anterior cruciate ligament, without discontinuity, consistent with myxoid degeneration.
- Degeneration of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus (grade II). An oblique tear extending to the tibial surface is noted at the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus. A small radial tear at the body–anterior horn junction of the lateral meniscus.
- Thinning of the cartilage at the medial portion of the lateral tibial plateau, with a small subchondral lesion measuring 2.7 mm, with accompanying bone edema.
- Small intra-articular fluid collection with two foci of thickened synovium between the medial meniscus–medial collateral ligament and medial femoral condyle, and between the lateral meniscus and iliotibial band–lateral femoral condyle.
- The extensor mechanism and the patellofemoral joint appear normal.

CONCLUSION
The two foci of synovitis in combination with small subchondral erosion at the tibial plateau raise suspicion of inflammatory arthritis. Rheumatological evaluation is recommended and possibly re-examination with contrast administration.

text: RIGHT KNEE MRI. Examination protocol: Multiplanar, multisequence. Findings: Grade III degeneration and a meniscal root tear were observed in the medial meniscus. The medial meniscus appears extruded medially. Periligamentous edema is present around the medial collateral ligament (grade I sprain). Grade II degeneration was observed in the lateral meniscus. The anterior cruciate ligament signal is diffusely increased, with focal thinning and irregularity in caliber proximally and distally (complete rupture). The posterior cruciate ligament and lateral collateral ligament are normal. Focal cartilage thinning at the medial facet level of the patellar cartilage and a subchondral millimetric cyst in the adjacent bone were observed (grade II chondromalacia). Mild osteophytic spurring in the bony structures forming the knee joint, joint space narrowing in the medial tibiofemoral compartment, and significant cartilage thinning were observed (findings of degenerative arthritis). Focal subchondral bone marrow edema at the level of the medial tibial plateau and diffuse bone marrow edema at the level of the medial femoral condyle were observed. Millimetric cysts at the level of the tibial intercondylar tubercle and lateral plateau with mild surrounding bone marrow edema were observed. A lobulated-contoured Baker's cyst measuring 8x8 mm was observed in the popliteal fossa. Peritendinous cysts were observed around the semitendinosus, gracilis, and semimembranosus tendons. A cystic lesion measuring 24x10 mm was observed at the inferior posterior level of the tibiofibular joint (ganglion cyst). Signal increase consistent with grade I-II strain in the popliteus muscle and a cyst approximately 1 cm in diameter at this level were observed.

text:
MRI OF THE RIGHT KNEE

TECHNIQUE
The examination was performed with pulse sequences: proton density with fat signal suppression and T2 gradient echo.

FINDINGS
- On evaluation of the menisci, simple degeneration is observed without evidence of tear.
- The ligamentous structures are intact.
- On evaluation of the articular cartilage, no findings are observed in the medial and lateral compartments. Degeneration is observed in the articular cartilage at the medial surface of the patella (ICRS III). Coexisting degenerative changes are present in the subcortical bone marrow at the mid-portion of the patella.
- A small fluid collection is observed intra-articularly with features of synovitis.
- A small Baker's synovial cyst is observed adjacent to the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle.
- Small ganglion cysts are observed at the tibiofibular junction.
- Small osteophytes are observed in the region of the intercondylar notch arising from the medial femoral condyle, as well as at the inferior pole of the patella.
- Suprapatellar edema is observed in the corresponding fat pad, which has a craniocaudal diameter of 2.5 cm.

CONCLUSION:
Findings of degenerative osteoarthritis at the patellofemoral joint, with findings particularly at the medial articular surface of the patella, with accompanying effusion and mild synovitis. The edema of the suprapatellar fat pad could be attributed to impingement of the quadriceps tendon against the femoral bone in the context of the aforementioned osteoarthritis.

text:
MRI KNEES

TECHNIQUE
The examination was performed with T1, T2 gradient echo and proton density pulse sequences with fat signal suppression.

RIGHT KNEE
On evaluation of the medial compartment, findings of degenerative osteoarthritis are observed with degenerative tear and subluxation of the meniscus, subchondral bone marrow edema, presence of marginal osteophytes and erosion of the articular cartilage up to ICRS 4.
On evaluation of the lateral compartment, the only finding noted is the presence of marginal osteophytes.
On evaluation of the patellofemoral compartment, significant degenerative osteoarthritis is observed with erosion of the articular cartilage in the patella and femoral trochlea up to ICRS 4, while the patella also demonstrates lateral subluxation.
Intra-articularly, a significant joint effusion is observed communicating with a large Baker's cyst adjacent to the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle with a craniocaudal diameter of 6 cm.
Within the joint effusion, multiple osteochondral loose bodies are observed.
It is also noted that the fabella presents a longitudinal diameter of 22 mm, most likely secondary to degenerative osteoarthritis.

LEFT KNEE
On evaluation of the medial compartment, degenerative osteoarthritis is observed with erosion of the articular cartilage up to ICRS 4, presence of subchondral bone marrow edema, presence of marginal osteophytes and degeneration and subluxation of the medial meniscus.
In the lateral joint space, marginal osteophytes are observed on the femoral and tibial condyle.
On evaluation of the patellofemoral compartment, findings of articular cartilage erosion in the patella and femoral trochlea up to ICRS 4 are observed with presence of subchondral bone marrow edema in the patella.
Intra-articularly, a moderate joint effusion is observed with the presence of a few loose bodies within it.
A small Baker's cyst is observed in the medial popliteal fossa.
The fabella presents increased dimensions (1.5 cm).

ACL.evidence: No mention of the ACL in either knee; report is focused entirely on degenerative disease.

MCL.evidence: No mention of the MCL or any collateral ligament injury in either knee.

Medial Meniscus.evidence: RIGHT: 'degenerative tear and subluxation of the meniscus'; LEFT: 'degeneration and subluxation of the medial meniscus' (no explicit tear on left, but right is unequivocal).

Lateral Meniscus.evidence: No lateral meniscal tear described in either knee; lateral compartments show only marginal osteophytes.

Medial OA.evidence: RIGHT: 'degenerative osteoarthritis…erosion of the articular cartilage up to ICRS 4'; LEFT: identical wording with ICRS 4 erosion.

Lateral OA.evidence: RIGHT: 'the only finding noted is the presence of marginal osteophytes'; LEFT: 'marginal osteophytes are observed on the femoral and tibial condyle.' No cartilage loss described.

PF OA.evidence: RIGHT: 'significant degenerative osteoarthritis…erosion of the articular cartilage in the patella and femoral trochlea up to ICRS 4'; LEFT: 'articular cartilage erosion in the patella and femoral trochlea up to ICRS 4.'

Effusion.evidence: RIGHT: 'a significant joint effusion is observed'; LEFT: 'a moderate joint effusion is observed.'

Synovitis.evidence: Not explicitly stated, but severe tricompartmental OA (ICRS 4), significant/moderate effusions, osteochondral loose bodies, and large Baker's cyst strongly imply reactive synovitis.

Baker's.evidence: RIGHT: 'a large Baker's cyst adjacent to the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle with a craniocaudal diameter of 6 cm'; LEFT: 'A small Baker's cyst is observed in the medial popliteal fossa.'

Gonarthrosis. Medial extrusion and grade III meniscopathy of the medial meniscus, grade III meniscopathy of the lateral meniscus. Fluid:
Moderate joint effusion with mild synovial thickening. Tiny amount of fluid in the pes anserine bursa. No popliteal cyst.

Bone contusions in the posterior aspect of the bilateral tibial plateau.

As above.

None

Findings:
There is a heterogeneous appearance of the bone marrow, more prominently involving the distal femur. There is no extra-osseous soft tissue component. There are similar but less marked changes involving the proximal tibia and fibula.
There is a small intra-articular effusion without a popliteal cyst. There is a multi-loculated ganglion cyst measuring 2 cm AP x 1.8 cm transverse x 1 cm craniocaudal at the level of the anterior intercondylar region. No evidence of an associated meniscal tear. The cyst appears to originate from the distal fibers of the anterior cruciate ligament.
There is prominence and fragmentation of the tibial tuberosity without bone edema, compatible with old Osgood-Schlatter disease.
Otherwise, the anterior cruciate ligament, the posterior cruciate ligament, the extensor mechanism, the medial collateral ligament, the semimembranosus, the popliteus muscle and tendon, the distal biceps femoris, the lateral collateral ligament, and the iliotibial band are unremarkable.
Conclusion:
1. There is no meniscal tear or anterior cruciate ligament injury.
2. Ganglion cyst at the level of the anterior intercondylar region that appears to originate from the anterior cruciate ligament. This could cause pain especially in full knee extension. Clinical correlation is recommended.
3. Sequelae of old Osgood-Schlatter disease.
4. Incidental finding of a heterogeneous bone marrow appearance. This is nonspecific and could represent red marrow reconversion. An infiltrative process is less likely but remains in the differential diagnosis. Hematological investigation is recommended.

Left knee pain. Patellofemoral chondropathy.
Findings:
No significant bone marrow signal abnormalities.
Cruciate and collateral ligaments within normal limits.
The lateral meniscus is of preserved morphology and signal, without signs of tear.
Increased central signal of the posterior horn and body of the medial meniscus that does not categorically contact the articular surface, without features of a tear.
Partial and near-full-thickness chondral ulcers of the central region of the weight-bearing zone of the medial femoral condyle. No significant joint effusion or popliteal cysts.

Chondropathy grade 2 and 3 lesions of the central region of the weight-bearing zone of the medial femoral condyle.
Chondropathy grade 3 and 4 lesions of the patella.
Mild proximal patellar tendinosis.

Others

MRI OF THE RIGHT KNEE

TECHNIQUE
The examination was performed with T1 and proton density pulse sequences with fat signal suppression.

FINDINGS
On evaluation of the lateral meniscus, the anterior cruciate ligament, and the collateral ligaments, no significant findings are observed.
Simple degeneration without tear at the anterior and posterior horns of the medial meniscus.
Myxoid degeneration is observed in the proximal half of the posterior cruciate ligament.
On evaluation of the extensor mechanism and the anterior compartment, an osteochondral lesion of degenerative origin is observed at the mid articular surface of the patella with significant cartilage thinning and subarticular bone marrow lesions in the patella, while at the lateral aspect of the patella, fissural erosions (fraying) are observed.
A moderate fluid collection is observed intra-articularly.
In the lateral aspect of the joint cavity, suprapatellarly, a synovial fold is observed along with the presence of small foci of fatty metaplasia of the synovium, which raises suspicion of an early "frond-like" lipoma (lipoma arborescens).
Prominent varicose venous dilatations are observed in the subcutaneous tissue of the medial aspect of the knee.

text: MRI findings: No MRI evidence of joint effusion. The bones forming the right knee joint are of normal shape and signal intensity. Osteophyte deposits on the condyles, most pronounced on the lateral femoral condyle and the lateral tibial condyle. Osteophytes also along the articular margins at the level of the patellofemoral joint. A bone cyst medially in the tibial epiphysis, beneath the intercondylar eminences. RIGHT KNEE MRI.
Examination protocol: Multiplanar, multisequence.
Findings:
The medial meniscus is extruded 4.5 mm medially in the knee joint. Maceration, volume loss, and complex tears are observed in the meniscus. Grade II degeneration is observed in the anterior and posterior horns and body of the lateral meniscus. Thickening and increased signal secondary to mucoid degeneration are observed in the anterior cruciate ligament. The posterior cruciate ligament and lateral collateral ligament are normal. Periligamentous edema is observed in the medial collateral ligament (grade I sprain). Loss of cartilage integrity is observed on the medial facet of the patella. Cartilage thinning and subchondral bone marrow edema are observed on the lateral facet. Increased fluid is observed in the suprapatellar bursa and knee joint space. An extra-articular ganglion cyst measuring 2.5x1.5 cm is observed adjacent to the postero-superior aspect of the medial femoral condyle. A tear in the posterior knee joint capsule and a 2x1.5 cm ganglion cyst associated with the tear are observed. A subcortical cyst measuring 1 cm in diameter is observed at the anterior tibial intercondylar eminence at the level of the anterior cruciate ligament insertion. Edema is observed in the peripatellar subcutaneous fat tissue. Joint space narrowing in the medial tibiofemoral compartment, subchondral sclerosis, edema, and degenerative cysts on the bone surfaces adjacent to the joint are observed. Cartilage destruction in the femoral and tibial cartilage at this level is observed. Findings are interpreted in favor of degenerative arthritis. An osteochondral defect measuring 6x4 mm is observed in the subchondral area of the lateral femoral condyle. Central-marginal osteophyte formation is observed in all three compartments of the knee joint.
Conclusion: Gonarthrosis, medial extrusion, maceration, volume loss, and complex tears of the medial meniscus, grade II meniscopathy of the lateral meniscus, mucoid degeneration of the anterior cruciate ligament, grade I sprain of the medial collateral ligament, suprapatellar bursitis, synovitis of the knee joint, extra-articular ganglion cyst, subcortical cyst at the tibial intercondylar eminence, prepatellar subcutaneous edema, tear of the posterior knee joint capsule and ganglion cyst associated with the tear, grade III chondromalacia of the medial facet and grade II chondromalacia of the lateral facet of the patella.

Exam Type: MRI KNEE LEFT WO CONTRAST

Indication: Several week history of left knee pain after fall. Pain localized laterally. No prior surgery.
Comparison: No relevant prior studies available for comparison.

TECHNIQUE:
MRI of the left knee was performed on a 1.5 Tesla system with a dedicated knee coil in three planes (axial, sagittal, and coronal), using a standard non-contrast protocol.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:
Alignment is anatomic. No acute fracture or bone bruise. Mild degenerative subchondral cystic change at the anterior margin of the medial tibial plateau. Background marrow signal is normal without infiltrative marrow process. No aggressive osseous lesions. 

JOINT SPACE:
Minimal joint effusion. No intra-articular bodies. Small Baker's cyst.

MEDIAL COMPARTMENT:
Medial meniscus: Oblique undersurface tear involving the posterior body-horn junction and posterior horn medial meniscus with superimposed small 3 mm intrameniscal cyst formation of the posterior horn. Moderate extrusion of the body partially displaced within the meniscotibial recess.
Medial compartment cartilage: Scattered areas of low grade partial thickness cartilage loss along the central weightbearing medial femoral condyle and along the anterior medial tibial plateau.

LATERAL COMPARTMENT:
Lateral meniscus: Normal in morphology and signal.

Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL): Normal with both bundles intact.
Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL): Normal.

COLLATERAL LIGAMENTS & POSTEROLATERAL CORNER:
Medial collateral ligament (MCL): Intact.
Lateral collateral ligament (LCL) complex: Grade 2 sprain of the fibular collateral ligament proximally near the femoral attachment characterized by high-grade partial-thickness tearing and fiber irregularity and surrounding peritendinous edema. The iliotibial band, biceps femoris and popliteus tendon are intact. Popliteofibular ligament appears intact.

EXTENSOR MECHANISM:
Distal quadriceps tendon: No tendinosis or tear.
Patella tendon: No tendinosis or tear.
Medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) and patellar retinacula: Normal.
Patellofemoral tracking: No edema in superolateral Hoffa's fat pad. No lateral patellar tilt or translation. No patella alta. Normal patellar and trochlear morphology. Normal tibial tubercle-trochlear groove (TT-TG) distance measuring 8 mm.

MUSCLES/TENDONS:
No acute muscle strain or muscle atrophy. Visualized tendons not previously discussed are intact without tendinosis or tear.

SOFT TISSUES:
Moderate prepatellar subcutaneous soft tissue edema and non organized fluid, may reflect underlying soft tissue contusion in the setting of fall. No soft tissue mass. Normal popliteal neurovascular bundle.

2.	Oblique undersurface tear posterior body and posterior horn medial meniscus with moderate meniscal extrusion and partial displacement within the meniscotibial recess.
3.	Mild tricompartmental chondrosis.
4.	Small Baker cyst.
5.	Moderate anterior soft tissue edema likely representing contusion.

TECHNIQUE: The examination was performed with PD sequences with fat signal suppression, T1 and T2*.

FINDINGS:
- A large amount of fluid is identified within the joint with extension into the suprapatellar recess and the lateral recesses.
- On evaluation of the menisci, pathological signal and margin irregularity are identified in the medial meniscus, at the posterior horn and partly at the body. Meniscal material is observed anterior to the insertion of the transverse ligament at the anterior horn.
- The lateral meniscus appears normal.
- On evaluation of the ligamentous structures, the anterior cruciate ligament demonstrates diffusely pathological signal, consistent with mild myxoid degeneration, without disruption of fiber continuity. The posterior cruciate ligament and the collateral ligaments appear normal.
- On evaluation of the articular cartilage, a full-thickness defect measuring 7 mm in length is observed at the weight-bearing portion of the medial femoral condyle with accompanying bone marrow edema (ICRS 4).
- On evaluation of the extensor mechanism, a shallow femoral trochlea is identified (sulcus angle 159°). Additionally, a small focal degeneration is identified at the distal portion of the patellar tendon and at its medial aspect.
- Bone marrow edema is observed at the medial tibial epiphysis, with the articular surface intact.

CONCLUSION:
1. Microtrabecular insufficiency fracture of the medial tibial epiphysis (synonymous with "spontaneous osteonecrosis"), without collapse of the articular surface.
2. Moderate osteoarthritis of the medial compartment with degenerative tear of the medial meniscus, full-thickness cartilage defect at the medial femoral condyle, subarticular bone marrow edema, and joint effusion.

- A moderate joint effusion is recognized. Projecting synovial folds (plicae) at the superior part of the patellofemoral joint, possibly without clinical significance. Clinical correlation is recommended.
- Incidentally, a bony exostosis without edema at the present phase is seen at the region of insertion of the adductor magnus muscle at the superior part of the femoral condyle, possibly corresponding to an old injury.

Oblique inferiorly surfacing tear of the medial meniscus involving body and posterior horn with associated para meniscal cyst posteriorly.

Known mildly comminuted undisplaced avulsion fracture of the tibial tuberosity involving the distal ACL insertion, anteriorly the anterior horn root insertion of the lateral meniscus, as well as posteriorly the tibial insertion of both the posterior horn of medial and lateral menisci. The fracture involves the central portion of the medial tibial plateau articular surface anteriorly and posteriorly with articular surface collapse of 3 mm anteriorly and 5 mm posteriorly, as well as a step deformity of up to 2 mm posteriorly.

None.

TECHNIQUE: The examination was performed with T1, PD FS, T2me2d sequences.

- Significant amount of intra-articular effusion as well as presence of a large Baker's cyst, with a cephalocaudal dimension of 6.3 cm, extending cephalad anterior to the semimembranosus muscle with multicystic character.
- Numerous nodular free bodies of bony texture coexist intra-articularly, as well as within the Baker's cyst.
- The collateral ligaments and the cruciate ligament appear normal, as well as the medial meniscus.

CONCLUSION: Extensive degenerative changes mainly in the lateral compartment and to a lesser degree in the medial compartment and in the patellofemoral articulation, with accompanying secondary osteochondromatosis.
